word_order: SVO | Subjects precede finite verbs and objects follow them (e.g. 'He trained as an obstetrician', 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device').
fillers_and_hesitations: none observed (no overt hesitation particles in these written samples)
discourse_markers: subordinating conjunctions that introduce dependent clauses (although, because)
coordinating conjunctions that link independent clauses (and, but)
sentence-level adverbials/parentheticals that frame or comment on clauses (of course, in reality)
temporal/locative adverbials that open clauses (after the war, in 1959)
clause_boundary_signals: coordinating conjunctions introducing a new main clause (and, but)
subordinating conjunctions or complementizers that introduce dependent clauses (although, that)
relative pronouns introducing post-nominal clauses (which, that)
non_boundary_traps: prepositional/temporal adverbials that may appear clause-initial but attach to a clause (for over a thousand years, around 60 cases)
numerical/quantificational noun phrases that look like separate fragments (Eighteen percent of Venezuelans, sixty cases)
possessive/nominal modifiers and titles that precede a noun phrase (Sir Richard Branson's, the Apollo X command module)
parenthetical adverbials that resemble clause-openers but do not close the current clause (of course, in reality)
unstable_prefix_signals: scope-limiting particles whose scope is uncertain until the following material (only, just)
approximate numerals that can be refined or constrained by following context (around, about)
subordinators that can be temporal vs. concessive/contrastive until continuation is seen (while, although)
conditional introducers that delay the main assertion (if, once)
notes_for_prompt_writer: English in these samples is formal, SVO, with auxiliaries and modal verbs preceding main verbs and negation realized post-auxiliary (e.g. aren't trusted). Adjectives and possessives precede nouns; relative clauses are post-nominal and introduced by relative pronouns. Temporal and other adverbial phrases freely appear clause-initial and often attach to the nearest verb phrase; numerals and quantifiers occur inside noun phrases and can look like separate units. Phrasal verbs and verb+particle sequences (take out of his pocket) occur and should be treated as cohesive units for meaning.
